t: to cry out. To shout and pray.

as it says: against the adversary that oppresses you, and you shall sound the alarm with trumpets. And the continuation of the verse: 'and you shall be remembered before the Lord your God,' and the remembrance is accomplished by the blast of the trumpets together with a cry of prayer.
that is, anything that distresses you. 'The adversary that oppresses you' is interpreted here not as meaning only an enemy, but as any trouble that comes.
of the ways of repentance. See also Hilchot Teshuvah 2:4.
and this is what will cause them to remove the trouble from themselves. Through their repenting.
from the way of the world. From the natural course of things.
it happened by chance. It occurred accidentally.
this is a path of cruelty. Hardness of heart.
and the trouble will increase. The present trouble will continue and further troubles will come.
if you say it is chance. It came by accident and not by God's providence.
the fury of that chance. An additional trouble following the thought that the trouble was accidental.
and by rabbinic law. By enactment of the Sages.
the shofar is shorter. The blast of the shofar is shorter than the blast of the trumpets.

for the mitzvah of the day is with trumpets. On days of trouble the main mitzvah is blowing the trumpets, as it says (Numbers 10:9) 'and you shall sound the alarm with trumpets' (unlike Rosh Hashanah, on which the main mitzvah is with the shofar; see Hilchot Shofar 1:2).
together. At the same time.
before the King. In the Temple.
for most of the community cannot sustain this. And the court may not impose a decree that most of the community cannot sustain (Hilchot Mamrim 2:5).

and they do not initially decree a fast except on Monday. When beginning a series of fasts they start it on Monday specifically, for if they set the first fast close to Shabbat, it might cause prices to rise (see Commentary to the Mishnah Ta'anit 2:9, and Yad Peshutah, who discusses this at length).

and so in this order: Monday, Thursday, and Monday. Each time they decree an additional series they begin on Monday (and in the middle fasts for withholding of rain, since they are a continuation of the first series, they begin on a Thursday of the week; Yad Peshutah; and see below 3:3).
they do not decree a fast on the community on Shabbatot or on festivals. See Hilchot Shabbat 30:12, Hilchot Yom Tov 6:10.
unless it was a city surrounded by gentiles etc.. See also Hilchot Shabbat 2:24.
a ship tossed at sea. That was caught in a storm and is in danger of sinking.
an evil spirit. Mental illness.

but they do not blow unless they blew to gather the people etc.. Although the Sages were strict about blowing on Shabbat because of the 'shevut' prohibition (see Hilchot Shofar 2:6), they permitted blowing for the sake of help and rescue.
on Chanukah and Purim. See Hilchot Megillah ve-Chanukah 2:13, 3:3.
on the intermediate days of a festival. See Hilchot Yom Tov 6:22.
pregnant women. Women who are expecting.

except for the fasts for rain, as will be explained. For in some of the fasts for withholding of rain, pregnant and nursing women fast, and it is also forbidden to eat from the evening before; see below 3:3-6.
but if he slept, he may not get up and eat. See also below 3:3.

and he says 'Answer us' etc. in every prayer that he prays. He adds in the Shemoneh Esrei, in the blessing 'Who hears prayer,' a supplication for the fast day called 'Aneinu' (see Hilchot Tefillah 2:14; for the text of the prayer see Seder ha-Tefillot, Blessings of the Amidah, 5).
and he should not fast on Shabbatot. Except for a fast over a dream (see below, halacha 12).
and resolves in his heart. Decides in his mind.
and he does not need intention for each and every day from while it is still day. He does not need a separate acceptance of the fast from while it is still day for each day on its own.
he changed his mind to fast on Monday. He regretted and decided to fast on the second day as well.
even though he stayed overnight in his fast. That he did not eat between the first day and the second.
for this is not a fast at all. Because he did not accept it while it was still day.
and he should examine them. For something that needs correcting.
because he nullified the delight of Shabbat. See Hilchot Shabbat 30:7-9.
and decided to fast. Decided and took upon himself to fast.
delicacies. Luxuries.
and he is permitted to taste the dish, even up to a revi'it. But not more than that (see Hilchot Berakhot 1:2).
he completes his fast. He finishes it as usual.
one who forgot and ate and drank should not appear before them. Because it is evident that he ate and the people of the city would envy him.
and he should not treat himself to delicacies. He should not say: since I ate a little I will eat a lot; rather he should fast with them.
and rain fell for them. In the amount detailed below 4:19.

and they recite the Great Hallel. From 'Give thanks to the Lord for He is good' to the end of the chapter (Psalm 136; see Commentary to the Mishnah Ta'anit 3:5; and compare Hilchot Chametz u-Matzah 8:10).
since most of the day has passed in holiness. For they have already fasted most of the day.
with the blessings and curses in the Torah. Those stated in Parashat Bechukotai (Leviticus 26:3-46; and see also Hilchot Tefillah 13:18).
the locust. That damages grain.
the chasil. A kind of locust.
blight. A drying plague in grain.
mildew. A plague that turns grain yellow-green.
the collapsing. Of houses. The details of these troubles and their definitions will be explained later in the chapter.
and sound the alarm. With trumpets.
but they ask for mercy for them. In prayer.
as we said. Above 1:6.
decree of persecution. A decree to abolish the religion or one of the commandments (Hilchot Yesodei ha-Torah 5:3).
five hundred foot soldiers. Men, not counting women, children, and the elderly.
and three of them died. Died in it.
and likewise according to this calculation. According to this ratio.

and the women, children, and elderly who ceased from work are not included in the number of the people of the city for this purpose. Because their constitution is naturally weak and they are more likely to die.
when it is sent. From heaven and harms in an unnatural way.
if it appeared in the city by day, it is a sent beast. For it is not its way to be found in the city by day.
if it saw two people and did not flee from them, it is a sent beast. Because normally it flees.
a field adjacent to a marsh. A field next to a meadow, the natural habitat of wild animals.
if it did not chase after them, it is not sent. Even though it did not flee, because it is not its way to flee when it is near a marsh.
unless it mauled both and ate one of them. This shows that it mauled not because of hunger.
the deserted places. The desolate places.
since they are places of troops of beasts. And the beasts found there are not accustomed to fear people.
and if it did not reach this measure, it is not sent. Even though it does not flee, or it mauled two and ate one, and the like.
for these are people who endangered themselves and came to the place of the beasts. And this does not fall under the category of a sent beast.
over the locust and the chasil... they fast and sound the alarm over them. Because they damage grain.
the gov. A kind of locust.
but for the chagav they do not fast or sound the alarm. For it does not damage grain like the other kinds.
as much as the mouth of an oven. That these plagues began in grain of an amount from which one would normally bake bread to fill the mouth of an oven.
sound walls. Strong ones, not likely to fall.
that are not standing beside a river. Because water weakens walls standing beside a river and they are likely to fall.
the earthquake. A quake.
askara. A contagious throat disease (diphtheria).
charchur. A disease that heats the body (see Deuteronomy 28:22).
moist itch. A disease that causes irritation and itching of the skin; the cure of moist itch is harder than that of dry itch.
and likewise moist itch... and if it spread among most of the community. Even though they did not die of it.

that goods became cheap on which most of the livelihood of the people of that city depends. That the value fell of things from which the people of the city normally make their living by trade, and consequently they have to sell them at a great loss.
the merchant. The trader.
and sound the alarm over it. In prayer (see above, halacha 2).
and they cry out over it on Shabbat. As above, halacha 1.
if rains increased upon them until they distressed them. Floods and the like.
because it is a mountainous land. And stones can be quarried from them for houses.
and their houses are built of stone. And they do not collapse easily because of the abundance of rain.
or until the plants dried up. After which the rains are of no benefit.

and likewise if the time of Passover arrived or was near in the Land of Israel, which is the time of the blossoming of trees there, and rain did not fall. That the rain suited to trees (heavy rain) did not fall, but rain of another kind that benefits plants and the like (light rain).
and the pits. Excavations in the ground.
at all. In general.
and all the disciples are fit for this. And they are permitted to fast too, unlike the rest of the people, who are not permitted to fast because it looks like pride.
and they are permitted to eat and drink at night. Before the fast, because the fast begins at dawn (see above 1:8).

the men of the mishmar. The priestly watch assigned that week to the Temple service. Each mishmar was divided into ancestral houses, each of which served on one day of that week (see Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 4:3, 4:11). In these fasts, all the men of the mishmar do not fast, so that they will have the strength to assist the men of the ancestral house assigned to the service of that day.
and they were not answered. Rain did not fall.
they eat and drink while it is still day. They stop eating at sunset and are forbidden to eat at night.
they fast part of the day and do not complete it. They do not fast until the end of the day.
they should not fast at all. So that they will not become weak from the fast and be disturbed in their work.
and decided not to eat. Resolved that he will not eat any more.

they are forbidden to work by day and permitted at night. Unlike Yom Kippur, on which work is forbidden at night as well (see Hilchot Shevitat Asor 1:6), and unlike Tisha B'Av, on which the prohibition of work depends on custom (below 5:10).

and they are forbidden to bathe the whole body in hot water, but the face, hands, and feet are permitted. Even in hot water, unlike a mourner, who is forbidden even to bathe part of the body in hot water (Hilchot Avel 5:4), and unlike Tisha B'Av and Yom Kippur, when even washing a single limb in cold water is forbidden (below 5:10, Hilchot Shevitat Asor 3:1).
and they are forbidden to anoint. Applying oil and the like to the skin.

and if it is to remove filth, it is permitted. For it is not anointing for pleasure (see below 5:10, Hilchot Avel 5:4), unlike Yom Kippur, on which even anointing that is not for pleasure is forbidden (Hilchot Shevitat Asor 3:9).
and they are forbidden marital relations. See ibid. 1:5.
and to wear sandals in the city, but on the road it is permitted to wear them. So that his feet will not be injured.
and these additional ones. These seven fasts beyond the fasts that preceded them.
they sound the alarm. With the shofar.
and they bring down an elder. Before the ark (the order of the prayer on these fasts is detailed below, chapter 4).
they close up toward evening and open the shops. They half-close the doors a little and do not open them wide.
out of respect for Shabbat. Because the shopping is for the honor and delight of Shabbat.
and if the shop has two doors, he opens one and locks one. On Thursday.
a stall in front of it. A shelf or table on which goods are placed.
he opens as usual on Thursday. Both doors of the shop, because the stall blocks the doorways.
and in building for joy... and in planting for joy. But building for dwelling and planting for eating the fruit or for a livelihood is permitted (Commentary to the Mishnah Ta'anit 1:7).
painting and engraving. The builder's engraving in plaster or stone to decorate the walls of the house (see Commentary to the Mishnah Middot 4:6).
such as kinds of myrtle and kinds of aloes. Kinds of spices.
has not fulfilled the mitzvah of being fruitful and multiplying. Who has no son and daughter (see Hilchot Ishut 15:4).
and Torah scholars do not greet. At all.
they answer him with a low voice and a heavy head. So that he is not hurt, and he will understand that they act this way because of the fast (and see below 5:11).
Torah scholars go back and fast on their own. After these fasts have passed and rain has not fallen.
until the Nisan of the equinox ends. Explained in the next halacha.
and they stop for Rosh Chodesh and Purim. If one of these fast days falls on Rosh Chodesh or Purim, they do not fast on it (see above 1:7).
the Nisan of the equinox ended. The Nisan mentioned here is not the month of Nisan, but the period when the sun is in the sign of Aries (see Hilchot Kiddush ha-Chodesh 9:3).
and that is when the sun reaches the beginning of the sign of Taurus. Which is the sign that follows Aries (see ibid. 11:9).
since it did not fall at all from the beginning of the year. But if rain fell earlier, the falling of rain after the Nisan equinox is not a sign of a curse.
and anything similar to it. Countries whose climate is similar to the climate of the Land of Israel.

and they wait about seven days after that. Just as in the Land of Israel the community fasts begin about seven days after the individuals finish fasting (see above, halacha 2), so too outside the Land of Israel.
and its law is like that of the other fasts. That they are forbidden only eating and drinking and are not forbidden bathing, wearing sandals, and the other things mentioned above, halacha 4.

for they do not decree on the community... except in the Land of Israel alone. For only in the Land of Israel are there ordained judges or a Nasi whose decree is accepted by all Israel (Ramban, cited in Beit Yosef).
of the last seven fasts for rain. Mentioned above 3:5-7.
ashes from a burning. Ashes from a fire.
to accustom to weeping. To bring about weeping.
so that they will be ashamed. For they do not give to themselves.
they stand among them while they are sitting. While they are sitting (and afterward they stand to pray, below, halacha 3).
a man of form. A handsome man or a man of stature (Rashi, Ta'anit 16a); some explain that it means a man famous for excellence and piety (Meiri there), or a man who knows scripture (Rosh there 2:22).
words of subduing. Words of rebuke that subdue the heart and arouse a person to repentance.
it is not sackcloth and fasting that cause. The arousal of mercy and the nullification of the decree.
and in the Prophets. In the words of the prophets.

a man who is accustomed to prayer and accustomed to read the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings. These conditions, as well as a pleasant voice and age, apply to a prayer leader at all times (see Hilchot Tefillah 8:11), and the other conditions are additional for prayer on fast days (Commentary to the Mishnah Ta'anit 2:2).
and has a family to support and has no means. Burdened with children and has nothing with which to support them.
and no bad name came out about him in his youth, humble and pleasing to the people. So that the heart of the community will be whole with him (ibid.).
this is praiseworthy. And it is preferable to choose him as prayer leader over a young man who also has these qualities.
he begins and prays. The Shemoneh Esrei prayer.
until the blessing 'Redeemer of Israel'. And he does not begin this blessing as usual, but begins by reciting the Zichronot and Shofarot etc.

Zichronot and Shofarot appropriate to the trouble. Verses of remembrance and verses of shofar suited to that trouble, provided that he does not recite verses of remembrance of an individual or of punishment (similar to what is said on Rosh Hashanah; see Hilchot Shofar 3:7-9).
from the words of the Prophets. From the words of the prophets.
and from the Holy Writings. The books of the Writings.

He who answered Moses and your fathers at the Red Sea. In the exodus from Egypt when they cried out to the Lord, as it says: 'And the children of Israel cried out to the Lord' (Exodus 14:10), and soon after it says 'Stand firm and see the salvation of the Lord,' and the Holy One, blessed be He, split the Red Sea for Israel.
He who answered Joshua at Gilgal. When the wall of the city of Jericho fell and the Lord gave the city into the hand of Israel (Joshua 6:20).

He who answered Samuel at Mizpah. When the Philistines fought Israel, it says 'And Samuel cried out to the Lord for Israel' (1 Samuel 7:9), and afterward the Lord gave the Philistines into the hand of Israel.
He who answered Elijah on Mount Carmel. When Elijah the prophet fought the prophets of Baal and prayed 'Answer me, Lord, answer me' (1 Kings 18:37) and fire descended from heaven.

He who answered Jonah in the belly of the fish. When Jonah fled from his mission to prophesy to Nineveh, he was thrown into the sea and a fish swallowed him, and he prayed to the Lord from the belly of the fish (Jonah 2:2).

He who answered David and Solomon his son in Jerusalem. When Solomon tried to bring the Ark of the Covenant into the Temple and did not succeed, he prayed to the Lord and finally was answered in the merit of his father David (see 2 Chronicles 7:1), and this was also a sign that David's sin was forgiven (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 30a).
and he says 'Heal us, Lord, and we shall be healed'. The blessing after 'Redeemer of Israel,' which he interrupted.

and completes the prayer in order and they blow the trumpets. The blowing of the trumpets comes only after the conclusion of all the blessings (unlike the blowing in the Temple, which is after each and every blessing, as explained in the next halacha).
and this order is followed everywhere. Except on the Temple Mount, as explained in the next halacha.

and the synagogue attendant says to the blowers: blow, priests, blow. And they do not blow (or sound the teruah) immediately after this announcement, but only after the one praying finishes reciting the blessing.

and the one praying repeats and says etc.. In order to separate between the blasts and the saying of 'Blessed be the name' etc., so that it does not look as though they are blowing for this statement, which is a blessing in itself (Maggid Mishneh).
they blow the trumpets and the shofar as we said. Above 1:4.
they pray the Ne'ilah prayer everywhere. A special prayer for the fast day recited near sunset (see Hilchot Tefillah 1:7).
until when do they go down and the community stops the fasts. According to the details explained above 1:16.
once a handbreadth of rain has penetrated the depth of dry, uncultivated land. That the rainwater is absorbed to a depth of a handbreadth into dry soil, in which water is absorbed very slowly.
and in average land. Which is neither dry nor plowed.
and in cultivated land. A plowed field, in which water seeps in quickly.
there are there. There are.

and this will be a remembrance of our evil deeds and the deeds of our fathers, which were like our deeds now, until they caused them and us those troubles. For the deeds of our fathers caused the troubles of the destruction and exile, and because our deeds are like theirs, those troubles are still in force.

Gedaliah son of Ahikam was killed, and the remaining ember of Israel was extinguished, and their exile was brought to completion. After the destruction of the First Temple, Gedaliah was appointed governor over the remnant of Judah, and after several months he was killed. As a result the Jewish settlement in the Land of Israel ceased entirely and the exile was completed (Jeremiah 41:2).
the wicked Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, besieged Jerusalem. Before the destruction of the First Temple (2 Kings 25:1).
the tablets were broken. The tablets of the covenant, by Moses our teacher (Exodus 32:19; for the calculation of dates see Babylonian Talmud Ta'anit 28b).
and the daily offering was discontinued in the First Temple. As a result of the siege of Nebuchadnezzar (for the story see Jerusalem Talmud Ta'anit 4:5; and see also Babylonian Talmud Sotah 49a).
and the city was breached in the Second Destruction. Titus's soldiers succeeded in breaching the walls of besieged Jerusalem.
and the wicked Apostomos burned a Torah scroll and placed an idol in the Sanctuary. In the days of the Second Temple.
it was decreed upon Israel in the wilderness that they would not enter the land. As a result of the sin of the spies (Numbers 14:29-30).

and they had a great king, and all Israel and the great Sages thought that he was the Messiah king. In the time of Rabbi Akiva, the Sages thought that Bar Kokhba was the Messiah king, until he was killed and, following him, all were killed (see Hilchot Melakhim 11:3).

the wicked Turnus Rufus, one of the kings of Edom, plowed up the Sanctuary. One of the Roman governors in Judea after the destruction of the Second Temple, in whose time the Bar Kokhba revolt broke out, turned the site of the Sanctuary into a plowed field as a symbol of total destruction.
to fulfill 'Zion shall be plowed as a field'. By this act the prophecy of Jeremiah and Micah was fulfilled.
in the Prophets. In the words of the prophets.
the fast of the fourth month, this is the seventeenth of Tammuz. Which is the fourth month from the month of Nisan, from which the months of the year are counted.
and on all of them one eats and drinks at night. Until dawn (see above 1:8).
and all Israel are accustomed at these times to fast on the thirteenth of Adar. Although this fast is not mentioned explicitly in Scripture, nor in the Gemara.
they advance and fast on Thursday, which is the eleventh. And they do not postpone this fast because the days of Purim come immediately after it.
they do not sound the alarm. With trumpets, unlike the other community fasts (above 1:4).
and do not pray the Ne'ilah prayer. A special prayer for the fast day recited near sunset (see above 4:18).
but they read from the Torah in the morning and afternoon 'And Moses entreated'. See also Hilchot Tefillah 13:18.
and the week in which the Ninth of Av falls. The week in which Tisha B'Av occurs.
to cut hair. To get a haircut.
even linen garments. Even though the pressing is not noticeable in them.
not to eat meat this week. This week (but on Shabbat itself it is permitted even if it falls on the Ninth of Av itself, as explained below, halacha 8).
and there are places that were accustomed to stop slaughtering from the beginning of the month. For they were accustomed not to eat meat from the start of the month of Av.
and he should not eat meat. Even one who was not accustomed to refrain from it in the week in which the Ninth of Av falls, as mentioned above, halacha 6.
at the meal at which he stops eating. After which meal he stops eating (the 'concluding meal').
wine from the vat that is three days old or less. Wine that came out of the winepress three days ago or less; since it has not had time to ferment, it is not intoxicating and may be drunk.

and he eats salted meat that is three days old or more. Meat that was salted after slaughter and remained in salt for two days; from the third day on it may be eaten, since it does not have the actual taste of meat (compare Hilchot Mamrim 7:4).
and he should not eat two cooked dishes. Because this is a way of importance and pleasure.
when does this apply?. That one is forbidden these things that were mentioned for the concluding meal.
even though he stops eating at it. And does not eat anything after it.
and likewise the Ninth of Av itself when it falls on Shabbat. And the fast is postponed to Sunday (see above, halacha 5).
this is the measure for all the people. The laws of the concluding meal stated above.

and it is forbidden to bathe... and it is forbidden to anoint for pleasure, to wear sandals, and marital relations, like Yom Kippur. See Hilchot Shevitat Asor 1:5; for the details of the laws see ibid. chapter 3.
and everywhere Torah scholars refrain from work on it. Even in a place where it is the custom to work.
Torah scholars do not greet one another on the Ninth of Av. Just as a mourner is forbidden to greet (see Hilchot Avel 5:20).
pained. In pain.
like mourners for a mother. Like a person mourning deeply for his mother (based on Psalms 35:14; in some manuscripts the reading is 'like mourners').
they answer him with a low voice and a heavy head. So that he is not hurt (and see above 3:8).
and it is forbidden to read the Torah on the Ninth of Av. Just as a mourner is forbidden to study Torah (see Hilchot Avel 5:15).
and the Lamentations. The Book of Lamentations.
and the evil things in Jeremiah. The prophecies of doom and not the prophecies of consolation.
and some Sages are accustomed not to put on tefillin on it. Like a mourner who does not put on tefillin on the first day of his mourning (see ibid. 4:9).
he plasters and leaves a mark like the building of kings. After plastering, the builder engraves in plaster or stone to decorate the walls of the house (see Commentary to the Mishnah Middot 4:6).
he leaves out a little of it. That he does not put on the table all the dishes that are usually put, but leaves out one of the kinds of dish.
and leaves an empty place without one of the bowls that it is fitting to put there. So that it will be noticeable on the table that he left out one of the dishes.
she removes one kind of the jewelry that they customarily wear. And she does not wear it.
they decreed not to play any musical instruments. Even not over wine.

singing with the mouth over wine is forbidden. Singing without musical instruments accompanied by drinking wine; but without drinking wine it is permitted to sing with the mouth (and see Responsa of Rambam 224).
and all Israel are already accustomed to say words of praise... over wine. With the mouth, without musical instruments.
and afterward they decreed. Not immediately after the destruction but in a later generation (see Mishnah Sotah 9:15).
crowns of bridegrooms. A decoration or ornament that was customarily placed on the head of the bridegroom.
but one of gedil. Woven wool.
and he tears. His garment (see Hilchot Avel 9:2).
and if he encountered the Temple first. That he directly saw the site of the Temple without seeing Jerusalem.
and adds to the tear for Jerusalem. And he need not make another tear (see Pesakim ve-Shittot).
by hand. And not with a tool (like tearing for a father and mother; see Hilchot Avel 8:3).
and standing. Like all tears (ibid. 8:1).
and he may never mend these tears. He is not permitted to sew the tear with a straight stitch and restore the garment to its former state; see also ibid. 9:3.
but he may sew them loosely, stitch them, gather them, and sew them like ladders. Kinds of stitching that are not straight and do not join the garment as it was, so that the tear remains noticeable.
he tears again. Another tear.
